title: ThreadVault Actual User Journey Architecture
evidence_basis: Static review of the current workspace source after separating DSA workflow helpers into services/. Automated tests cover the extracted helpers; this artifact does not claim a fresh browser-driven runtime exercise.
purpose: Canonical, source-grounded content for an interactive architecture and user-journey diagram. This file is the authority for program behavior represented by the diagram.

journey: Seller product listing and image upload
scope.runtime: Local Flask application connected to MariaDB. Flask can serve the static pages directly; optional Apache can serve static content and proxy supported paths.

components.name: Customer browser
components.description: Uses the storefront and customer account pages. Account identity is represented by the Flask session cookie; the browser cart is stored separately in localStorage.

components.name: Seller browser
components.description: Uses the seller portal to register, manage the seller's own listings, inspect order items, advance fulfillment status, and undo the seller's latest eligible status change.

components.name: Storefront browser logic
components.description: Loads the catalog, renders product browsing UI, filters and sorts in the browser, manages the cart, and submits checkout.

components.name: Customer account browser logic
components.description: Submits customer login and registration, checks the current session, loads customer orders, and logs out.

components.name: Seller portal browser logic
components.description: Submits seller login and registration, loads seller products and orders, parses size stock input, uploads images, saves listings, changes order-item status, and requests undo.

components.name: Flask application
components.description: Serves the pages and API, validates requests, enforces role checks, calls database-independent workflow services, and persists marketplace state.

components.name: DSA workflow services
components.description: Database-independent functions apply the custom DSA implementations to validated checkout lines, seller work rows, status history, and catalog records. Flask routes own HTTP handling, authorization, database access, and transactions.

components.name: MariaDB
components.description: Persistent storage for accounts, seller products, stock by size, orders, order items, and status-change history.

components.name: Linked FIFO Queue
components.description: order_lines_in_sequence enqueues validated checkout lines and dequeues them in request order. The Flask route performs the stock checks and database updates after receiving this ordered list.

components.name: Binary min-heap PriorityQueue
components.description: order_work_list inserts seller order-item rows with priority tuple (priority rank, order_id, item_id), then extracts them in that order.

components.name: Linked LIFO Stack
components.description: latest_undoable pushes eligible history rows supplied in ascending ID order and pops the latest row. The Flask route then verifies and persists the restoration.

components.name: Catalog search and sorting algorithms
components.description: search_catalog uses linear_search_all when a query is supplied, then sort_catalog uses merge_sort by case-folded product name. Browser-side filters and price sorting are separate JavaScript behavior.

components.name: Legacy catalog and image files
components.description: legacy_products reads products.json and adds legacy entries and image-backed brand entries. These legacy products have no checkout price or stock and are browse-only.

components.name: Uploaded product images
components.description: upload_product_image saves accepted image uploads under static/uploads using a generated UUID filename. The returned image URL can be stored on a product listing.

components.name: Browser localStorage cart
components.description: shop.js stores cart lines under localStorage key your-brand-cart. This is temporary browser state, not an order or database record.

components.name: Flask session cookie
components.description: Registration and login clear and populate Flask session fields. The default Flask session is cookie-based; there is no session table in schema.sql.

relationships: A seller owns products and is recorded as the seller on their order items.
Products have product_stock rows and can be referenced by order_items.

database_entities.purpose: Quantity available per product and size.
relationships: Composite primary key is (product_id, size). product_id references products.id.

database_entities.purpose: Customer order header and processing priority.
Purchased product-and-size lines, seller association, price snapshot, and current fulfillment status.
relationships: References orders.id, products.id, and users.id as seller.
Status is read by the customer history and seller portal.

database_entities.purpose: Audit trail of seller status transitions and undo markers.

journey.title: Customer creates an account
journey.entry: Customer submits the customer registration form in static/account.html.

steps.action: Builds a payload from the customer form and calls sendAccountRequest('/api/auth/register', payload).
steps.request: POST /api/auth/register with role customer, display_name, email, and password.
steps.persistence: INSERT users with a Werkzeug generate_password_hash password hash, then commit.
steps.result: Flask clears and sets the session, calls current_account(), and returns the user with HTTP 201.

journey.output: A users row with role customer and an active Flask session cookie.

journey.title: Seller creates an account
journey.entry: Seller submits the seller registration form in static/seller.html.

steps.action: Serializes the seller form and calls api('/api/auth/register').
steps.request: POST /api/auth/register with role seller, display_name, shop_name, email, and password.
steps.persistence: INSERT users with a password hash and shop_name, then commit.
steps.result: Flask clears and sets the session, calls current_account(), and returns the user with HTTP 201. loadSellerAccount() then checks GET /api/auth/me.

journey.output: A users row with role seller and shop_name, and an active Flask session cookie.

journey.title: Returning customer or seller signs in

steps.action: Looks up the normalized email, verifies the stored password hash, clears the prior session, and stores the signed-in user's fields in the Flask session.
steps.result: Returns the current account; account.js then calls loadCustomerAccount() to load customer order history when the role is customer.

steps.action: Looks up the normalized email, verifies the stored password hash, clears the prior session, and stores the signed-in user's fields in the Flask session.
steps.result: Returns the current account; seller.js then calls loadSellerAccount() to load seller products and orders when the role is seller.

journey.output: An authenticated Flask session for the account role. A login replaces the identity in the current browser session.
journey.note: The customer login form is on account.html and the seller login form is on seller.html.

journey.title: Seller creates and manages a product listing

steps.action: Checks /api/auth/me and loads products and orders for the signed-in seller.
steps.persistence: Reads seller-owned active products and product_stock from MariaDB.

steps.function: seller.js productForm submit listener then parseStock()
steps.action: Converts lines such as S:5 to size and quantity objects and sends the product payload.
steps.persistence: Inserts products and product_stock rows in a database transaction and commits.
steps.result: Returns the new product id, then seller.js refreshes its workspace.

steps.action: Uploads selected image as multipart form data.
steps.persistence: Checks allowed image extension and MIME type, saves a UUID-named file in static/uploads, returns image_url.

steps.action: Validates seller ownership under a row lock, updates listing fields, replaces product_stock rows, then commits.
Sets active to FALSE for the signed-in seller's active listing; this is a soft delete preserving references from past orders.

journey.output: A products row and associated product_stock rows keyed to the seller. Optional uploaded image is saved under static/uploads and its URL can be used by the product.

journey.title: Customer browses products

data_sources: Active seller listings and stock from MariaDB.
Legacy products from products.json and available images under assets/.
algorithms: services.catalog.search_catalog() uses linear_search_all() only if the q query parameter is non-empty.
services.catalog.sort_catalog() uses merge_sort() to order the resulting catalog by case-folded product name.
steps.result: JSON catalog consumed by renderCategories() and render() in shop.js.

steps.action: Applies interactive brand, category, and text filtering, and optional price sorting in browser JavaScript.
steps.important_distinction: These live UI controls use JavaScript array operations, not the custom Python linear search or merge sort.

steps.action: Adds legacy catalog entries with no price and no stock; shop.js displays them as not currently purchasable.

journey.output: Customer sees active database listings and legacy browse-only products. Purchasable items require an available seller listing with price and stock sizes.

journey.title: Customer builds a cart

steps.action: Adds or increments a line identified by product id and size. The browser limits a line quantity to 10.
steps.storage: save() writes cart JSON to localStorage key your-brand-cart.

journey.output: Browser-local cart lines; no MariaDB order is created until checkout.

journey.title: Customer checks out

steps.request: POST /api/orders with priority and cart items containing product_id, size, and quantity.
steps.validation: Requires non-empty items, priority urgent/express/standard, integer product ids, non-empty sizes, and integer quantities from 1 through 10.
steps.dsa: services.ordering.order_lines_in_sequence() enqueues validated items in dsa.queue.Queue and dequeues them FIFO. The Flask route performs database stock checks and updates afterward.
database_sequence: For each item, SELECT matching product and product_stock row FOR UPDATE.
Reject missing/inactive product or insufficient size stock.
Decrement stock and insert order_items with seller_id and unit_price snapshot.
Commit all order and stock changes together.
steps.failure: A stock or availability ValueError triggers rollback and HTTP 409. Invalid request data returns HTTP 400. A role mismatch returns HTTP 401.
steps.success: Returns HTTP 201 with order_id, pending status, and priority. shop.js clears the localStorage cart and shows confirmation.

journey.output: Persisted orders and order_items, reduced product_stock, and initial pending status for each item.

journey.title: Seller fulfills order items

steps.function: seller.js loadOrders() calls GET /api/seller/orders; app.py seller_orders()
steps.action: Selects order items assigned to the current seller, then calls services.fulfillment.order_work_list() to order the rows through PriorityQueue.
steps.priority_key: (priority rank, order_id, item_id), where urgent ranks before express, then standard.
steps.note: The priority queue orders the returned work list. A seller still initiates each status change.

steps.function: seller.js order update handler calls PATCH /api/seller/order-items/<item_id>; app.py update_order_item(item_id)
steps.action: Allows exactly one forward step, pending to processing or processing to fulfilled. Locks the item row, updates order_items.status, inserts order_status_history, and commits.

steps.function: seller.js undo-status click handler calls POST /api/seller/orders/undo-last-status; app.py undo_last_status()
steps.action: Loads this seller's not-yet-undone history ordered by id, calls services.fulfillment.latest_undoable() to use Stack and select the latest event, then locks the item, verifies current status equals event new_status, restores old_status, marks undone_at, and commits.
steps.failure: Returns HTTP 409 if there is no eligible event or the item's current status no longer matches the event.

journey.output: Current status is stored on order_items; each status change and undo marker is recorded in order_status_history.

journey.title: Customer views order status

steps.function: account.js loadCustomerAccount() calls GET /api/auth/me then GET /api/orders; app.py current_account() then customer_orders()
steps.action: The API selects the signed-in customer's order items, product names, seller shop names, unit prices, and current statuses.
steps.result: account.js renders order item details and current fulfillment status.
steps.shared_state: Reads order_items.status, the same field updated by the seller fulfillment routes.

journey.output: Customer sees current item-level order history and statuses.

connections.label: users.id and customer role/session authorize checkout
users.id and seller role/session identify listing owner
products and product_stock become the purchasable catalog
Customer selects a product and size into browser-local cart
Cart lines are submitted as checkout items
orders and order_items persist seller_id, priority, and pending status
Customer history reads the current order_items.status

system_rules: Customer and seller accounts use the same users table but separate role values. A role-protected route checks the role in the active Flask session.
Registration and login clear the current session before setting the new identity. Separate browser sessions are required to be signed in as a customer and seller at the same time.
The default Flask session is cookie-based. schema.sql has no session table.
Checkout is the point where a browser cart becomes a persisted order. Before then, the cart is localStorage state.
The checkout Queue is request-local and demonstrates FIFO ordering of validated lines; it is not a persistent or asynchronous job queue.
Checkout stock validation, stock decrements, order creation, and order-item inserts are committed together or rolled back on a handled availability/stock failure.
Order processing priority is for seller queue order only; it does not promise a delivery time.
Order status progresses pending to processing to fulfilled. The seller can request undo of the latest eligible status-change event.
DSA workflow helpers in services/ operate on in-memory values only; app.py retains HTTP, authorization, SQL, and transaction responsibilities.
Legacy products from products.json are browse-only because they have no price and no stock.
No payment, shipping label, payout, email, or production deployment integration is implemented.
The browser's live filtering and price sorting are JavaScript built-ins; custom Python search and merge sort are used by list_products for API catalog processing.

diagram_specification.deliverable: A self-contained interactive HTML page that visually explains the entire actual user journey and opens details when a diagram part is clicked.
diagram_specification.audience: A reader learning the system and tracing how a real customer and seller use the program.
layout: Show the journey in connected stages: account creation, seller listing, catalog browsing, cart and checkout, seller fulfillment and undo, customer order history.
Use distinct visual lanes or columns for customer browser, seller browser, Flask backend, application services, DSA modules, MariaDB, and file/browser storage.
Keep each stage readable at typical laptop width; allow panning, zooming, or responsive reflow rather than shrinking labels excessively.
Show persisted state and the handoff between stages, especially seller listing to catalog, checkout to fulfillment, and fulfillment status to customer order history.
interaction: Make each component and journey step clickable and keyboard accessible.
On click, show its title, plain-language explanation, actual function names, endpoint where applicable, important data read/written, and source file references.
Support selecting a journey step to highlight its incoming and outgoing connections.
Provide clear back/close behavior for the details panel and visible focus states.
visual_language: Differentiate actors, browser pages/scripts, backend functions, DSA structures, database tables, and file/browser storage using labels and consistent shapes or colors.
Use directed arrows for calls and data handoffs. Label arrows with route, function, or state passed.
Use solid arrows for actual HTTP or code calls and a distinct style for persisted-state handoffs between stages.
technical: Use only the facts and names in this JSON; do not invent routes, modules, functions, tables, runtime behavior, or business capabilities.
Keep the page self-contained and usable offline with no CDN, network API, build step, or framework dependency.
The HTML may transform this JSON into its visual model; do not manually replace its facts with duplicated conflicting content.
Include a small note that the source reflects static code review and is not a claim of runtime verification.
acceptance_criteria: A viewer can follow the customer path from registration to browsing, cart, checkout, and order history.
A viewer can follow the seller path from registration to listing, order queue, status update, and undo.
The arrows clearly communicate that checkout creates the database order items consumed by seller fulfillment, and that the customer history reads the same current item status.
Clicking every major diagram node reveals a useful explanation with its actual code references.
The diagram distinguishes browser-local cart data from MariaDB-persisted order data.
The diagram does not imply that payment or delivery is implemented.
